explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says, "So Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, received their inheritance." (Joshua 16:4) Two brothers, one big stretch of land. I bet the dinner table got loud over who had the better view.

Close, but Reuben isn't named in this verse. The verse names the two sons of Joseph who receive this land: Ephraim and Manasseh (Joshua 16:4). Joseph's name is right there in the sentence, so it's a good clue to hold onto.

Benjamin is a good name, but it isn't the one in this verse. The text says, "So Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, received their inheritance." (Joshua 16:4) So the blank is Manasseh. Easy to mix up when a whole parade of names is marching through a chapter.

explanations.answer: They do not drive them out
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says, "But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer." (Joshua 16:10) Gezer was a city in Ephraim's land. So the Canaanites stayed right there in it, like a houseguest who keeps saying he's leaving Thursday.

explanations.answer: They drive every one of them out
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. "But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer." (Joshua 16:10) Nobody cleared Gezer out. The Canaanites were still living there.

explanations.answer: They hand Gezer over to Manasseh
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about handing Gezer to Manasseh. What it does say is that Ephraim "did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer." (Joshua 16:10) The Canaanites stayed living among the Ephraimites. I'd have loved a cleaner ending too, but that's what the text gives us.

True. The text says, "So the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites to this day, but they are forced laborers." (Joshua 16:10) They stayed in Gezer, and they worked as forced laborers. Pay attention to that word "but," friend. It's doing a lot of work in that verse.

This one is true, so False misses it. The text says the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites "but they are forced laborers." (Joshua 16:10) They weren't driven out, and they weren't left free either. Forced laborers is exactly what the verse calls them.

explanations.answer: Because he was a man of war
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says Machir "had received Gilead and Bashan because Machir was a man of war." (Joshua 17:1) Machir was Manasseh's firstborn and the father of the Gileadites. The text gives the reason in one short phrase, no extra paperwork.

explanations.answer: Because he asked for it first
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the text doesn't say anything about asking first. It gives a different reason: Machir received Gilead and Bashan "because Machir was a man of war." (Joshua 17:1) No line, no number to take. Just a man of war.

explanations.answer: Because his clan was the largest
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions how big his clan was. It says Machir received Gilead and Bashan "because Machir was a man of war." (Joshua 17:1) That's the reason the verse gives, so I'm sticking to it.

explanations.answer: Eleazar the priest and Joshua and the leaders
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says, "They approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders." (Joshua 17:4) Five daughters walked up to the priest, Israel's leader and the leaders, and they brought their case right to the top. I'd have been hiding behind the cookie jar, but they walked right up.

explanations.answer: Caleb and the elders of the tribe of Judah
explanations.explanation: Caleb and Judah's elders aren't in this verse. The text says the daughters "approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders." (Joshua 17:4) That's who heard their case. It's a good reminder to check who is actually standing in the scene.

explanations.answer: Phinehas the priest and the sons of Levi
explanations.explanation: Phinehas isn't named in this verse. The priest here is Eleazar. The text says the daughters "approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders." (Joshua 17:4) So they went to Eleazar, Joshua and the leaders.

That's right. The daughters say, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers." (Joshua 17:4) Moses was Israel's leader before Joshua. They came with the LORD's command already in hand, which is a strong way to walk into a meeting.
Aaron's a big name, but he isn't the one in this verse. The daughters say, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers." (Joshua 17:4) So the name in the blank is Moses.

Jacob is a familiar name, but the daughters don't name him here. They say, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers." (Joshua 17:4) The blank is Moses. Careful, friend. Family-tree chapters will do that to you.

Joshua doesn't turn them away, so True misses it. The text says, "So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father's brothers, in keeping with the command of the LORD." (Joshua 17:4) They asked, and they received. I think those five walked out of there with a very good story.

False is right, friend. The text says, "So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father's brothers, in keeping with the command of the LORD." (Joshua 17:4) Nobody got sent home. They received land among their father's brothers.

explanations.answer: The rest of the sons of Manasseh
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says, "the land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh." (Joshua 17:6) The daughters of Zelophehad received an inheritance among Manasseh's sons, and Gilead went to those other sons. It's the land beyond the Jordan, a good way across from the rest of the shares.

Almost. The daughters did receive an inheritance "among his sons," but the text says Gilead "belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh." (Joshua 17:6) So Gilead goes to the rest of the sons. The daughters' share came in the ten shares.

explanations.answer: The clans of the tribe of Ephraim
explanations.explanation: Ephraim is Manasseh's brother, but Gilead isn't in Ephraim's share. The text says, "the land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh." (Joshua 17:6) That keeps it in Manasseh's family. Ephraim's land was mapped out back in chapter 16.

explanations.answer: No because the Canaanites are determined to stay
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The text says the descendants of Manasseh "were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land." (Joshua 17:12) The cities were assigned to Manasseh, but the Canaanites weren't packing. It's like holding the deed to a house while somebody sits in the living room.

explanations.answer: Yes and the Canaanites leave without a fight
explanations.explanation: The text says it didn't go that way. The descendants of Manasseh "were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land." (Joshua 17:12) The Canaanites didn't leave. They stayed.

explanations.answer: No because Joshua gives those cities to Asher
explanations.explanation: You've got the "No" right, but the reason isn't in the text. Joshua doesn't give the cities to Asher here. The text says Manasseh "were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land." (Joshua 17:12)

The Israelites did get stronger, but that's not the whole sentence. The text says, "they put the Canaanites to forced labor; but they failed to drive them out completely." (Joshua 17:13) So True misses it. The Canaanites stayed.

False is right, baker. The text says that when the Israelites grew stronger, "they put the Canaanites to forced labor; but they failed to drive them out completely." (Joshua 17:13) Stronger, yes. Finished, no. Pay attention to that "but."

explanations.answer: Why they got only one portion
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. They ask Joshua, "Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance?" (Joshua 17:14) They bring up the size of their family and say the LORD has blessed them. Joshua, Israel's leader, is the one on the receiving end of that question.

explanations.answer: Why their land has no springs
explanations.explanation: Springs never come up in this passage. They ask Joshua, "Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance?" (Joshua 17:14) It's about getting only one portion. Nothing about water.

explanations.answer: Why Judah got the best hills
explanations.explanation: The sons of Joseph don't mention Judah here. Their question is, "Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance?" (Joshua 17:14) They're talking about their own share. Nobody else's hills come up.

That's right. They say, "We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly." (Joshua 17:14) They credit the LORD for their big numbers. A crowded house is a good problem to have, friend.

The word isn't tested. The sons of Joseph say, "We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly." (Joshua 17:14) They're pointing to a blessing from the LORD as the reason for their numbers.
Humbled doesn't fit the verse. They say, "We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly." (Joshua 17:14) The word is blessed. That's the reason they give.

explanations.answer: Go clear land in the forest
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Joshua answers, "If you have so many people that the hill country of Ephraim is too small for you, go to the forest and clear for yourself an area in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim." (Joshua 17:15) The Perizzites and the Rephaim are peoples whose land is out there. So Joshua's answer is to go and clear the forest.

Joshua doesn't tell them to wait. He says to "go to the forest and clear for yourself an area in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim." (Joshua 17:15) It's an answer that needs an axe, not a calendar.

Joshua doesn't send them back across the Jordan. He says, "go to the forest and clear for yourself an area in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim." (Joshua 17:15) The plan is to clear forest, not to retreat.

That's it. They say, "all the Canaanites who live in the valley have iron chariots, both in Beth-shean with its towns and in the Valley of Jezreel." (Joshua 17:16) The Valley of Jezreel is a wide valley, and the chariots are the reason they bring it up. I think they were trying to say that the valley looked like a big challenge.
Gates isn't the word. The sons of Joseph say the Canaanites "have iron chariots, both in Beth-shean with its towns and in the Valley of Jezreel." (Joshua 17:16) The blank is chariots.

Idols don't come up in this verse. They say the Canaanites in the valley "have iron chariots, both in Beth-shean with its towns and in the Valley of Jezreel." (Joshua 17:16) It's chariots, and they're made of iron.

True, friend. Joshua says to the house of Joseph, "You have many people and great strength. You shall not have just one allotment." (Joshua 17:17) He had heard the complaint and he answers it. They're getting more than one.

That one's true, so False misses it. Joshua tells them, "You have many people and great strength. You shall not have just one allotment." (Joshua 17:17) He doesn't brush them off. He says they won't be limited to one.

You got it, baker. Joshua says, "Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out." (Joshua 17:18) He names the chariots and the strength right out loud, and he still says they can do it. Iron chariots on one side, a promise on the other.

Joshua doesn't say to leave them. He says, "Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out." (Joshua 17:18) That's a green light, not a stay-home note.

Making peace isn't what Joshua tells them. He says, "Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out." (Joshua 17:18) The word he gives them is that they can drive the Canaanites out.
